pr_title: Automatically mount virtual box shared folder when machine reboots
pr_body:
fixes https://github.com/hashicorp/vagrant/issues/11368
maybe supersedes https://github.com/hashicorp/vagrant/pull/11417

This is done by adding the mount to fstab
ref: https://askubuntu.com/questions/252853/how-to-mount-a-virtualbox-shared-folder-at-startup
pr_comments:
Hi @soapy1, thanks for the work! :+1: 
I cannot help but wonder however, if this is the best strategy for archiving persistent mounting, as it only works for Linux guests. My proposed solution in https://github.com/hashicorp/vagrant/pull/11417 works guest OS independent, as it uses VirtualBoxes build-in functionality for persistent volume mounting.

@Jasper-Ben good point! I spent some time trying to evaluate both methods of auto mounting after a reboot initiated from the host. While the upside of using the automounting feature on virtualbox is being OS independent, the downside is loosing control over the mount options of the folder. Using the virtual box flag does not preserve the owner/group of the folder between reboots. Users are currently able to specify these parameters and these setting should be respected between reboots that are initiated from inside the guest. These setting are able to be preserved using the fstab approach, so I think it should be used going forward. Note, that for windows auto mounting after reboot currently works, and for Darwin, only nfs and rsync synced folders are supported.

Hi @soapy1, I was not aware that auto-mounting does already work within Windows. Although I personally never really saw the need for assigning UID/GID for virtualboxes shared folders (I always used them the "virtualbox way" by adding the guests user(s) to the vboxsf group), I definitely can see that this feature might come in handy in advanced use cases. So I guess you are right, fstab is the way to go :smile: 

P.S.: I'm just happy to see this issue fixed so I can finally remove the ugly workaround for this issue from my Vagrantfile :laughing:

I'm going to lock this issue because it has been closed for _30 days_ ⏳. This helps our maintainers find and focus on the active issues.

If you have found a problem that seems similar to this, please open a new issue and complete the issue template so we can capture all the details necessary to investigate further.

### Expected behavior
Mounts should be present after reboot.

### Actual behavior
Rebooting the vm with the 'reboot' command within will break vagrant shared folders.  

This is problematic if the vm is being provisioned remotely (for example with Ansible), and for security reasons there is no ability to execute 'vagrant reload' on the host/metal.  vagrant reload has no problem, but we should be able to reboot the machine with the reboot command within.

As far as I can tell, this is a known issue by some others.
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/23894739/synced-folders-lost-when-rebooting-a-vagrant-machine-using-the-ansible-provision


### Steps to reproduce
1. ```vagrant up```
2. ```sudo reboot```
3. The shared folder is missing.

### References
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/23894739/synced-folders-lost-when-rebooting-a-vagrant-machine-using-the-ansible-provision
comments: @queglay  I guess so, but does this happen when [rebooting with a shell provisioner](https://www.vagrantup.com/docs/provisioning/shell.html#reboot)?

I posted a work-around to this in the linked StackOverflow question from above (see https://stackoverflow.com/a/61261742/937006) but I'm reproducing it here for posterity.

----

In case anyone else runs into this issue and finds this question like I did here's how I worked around the issue:

```
# -*- mode: ruby -*-
# vi: set ft=ruby :

Vagrant.configure("2") do |config|
  config.vm.box = "..."

  # create a shared folder for the top-level project directory at /vagrant
  # normally already configured but for some reason it isn't on these boxes
  # https://www.vagrantup.com/docs/synced-folders/virtualbox.html#automount
  # http://www.virtualbox.org/manual/ch04.html#sf_mount_auto
  config.vm.synced_folder ".", "/mnt/vagrant", id: "vagrant", automount: true
  config.vm.provision "shell", inline: "usermod -a -G vboxsf vagrant"
  config.vm.provision "shell", inline: "ln -sf /media/sf_vagrant /vagrant"

  # More settings omitted...
end
```
There's a few parts to this solution:

 1. The first line assigns a specific `id` of `vagrant` to the shared folder. This is important because the automatic mount functionality in VIrtualBox uses `/mnt/sf_<id>` by default. It also mounts the folder at `/mnt/vagrant` to keep it out of the way. Ideally you'd pick a more obscure location that's present on all of your VMs or just document not to use it there.
 2. The third line creates a symbolic link from the automatic mount location at `/mnt/sf_vagrant` to the usual place users expect the shared folder at `/vagrant`.
 3. The second line adds the `vagrant` user in the virtual machine to the `vboxsf` group. This is necessary to access files inside `/mnt/sf_vagrant` because the guest utilities mount the folder with `root:vboxsf` ownership. They also set appropriate file and directory modes so it works fine in practice but you do need to be a member of the `vboxsf` group.

This solution has the following benefits:

 * The mount at `/mnt/sf_vagrant` is automatically mounted by the virtualbox guest utilities after a reboot so `/vagrant` should always be available.
 * It does not require installing plugins or using any outside tools.

It has the following drawbacks:

 * Potential for unexpected behavior if users find and use the `/mnt/vagrant` mount. That mount will only be present if the virtual machine was most recently booted / rebooted through the `vagrant` console client otherwise it will not be present.
 * It requires a relatively recent version of VirtualBox and Vagrant.

review_comments: While the behavior ends up being the same, I think moving the `machine.config.vm.allow_fstab_modification` here makes it a bit clearer and less prone for accidental removal in the future.
